lessons.title: The neonatal period and passive immunity
lessons.html:
Why the first days decide so much

In every livestock enterprise, the juvenile phase – from birth or hatch to weaning or point of lay – carries the highest mortality risk and sets the growth curve for the rest of the animal's productive life. Calf, lamb, kid and piglet losses between birth and weaning are often the largest single drain on reproductive efficiency on South African farms. A manager or extension officer must therefore understand the biology of the newborn and the management levers that reduce losses.

Physiology of the newborn

  • Thermoregulation – newborns have limited fat reserves and a high surface-to-mass ratio. Lambs and kids born in cold, wet, windy Karoo or Highveld winters, and piglets without a heated creep, chill quickly; hypothermia then suppresses suckling and leads to starvation.
  • Energy reserves – brown fat and liver glycogen last only a short time; early suckling is essential.
  • Immune status – in ruminants and pigs the placenta does not transfer antibodies, so the newborn is born almost without immune protection.

Colostrum and passive transfer

Colostrum, the first milk, supplies concentrated antibodies (immunoglobulins), energy and vitamins. The newborn gut can absorb these large antibody molecules only for a short window after birth; absorption declines rapidly over the first day, which is why feeding colostrum as early as possible – ideally within the first few hours – is the single most important neonatal intervention. Failure of passive transfer is strongly associated with scours, navel infections and pneumonia.

Management implications:

  • Observe births and confirm that every newborn suckles; assist weak animals.
  • Keep a store of good-quality frozen colostrum, thawed gently (never boiled or microwaved hot, which destroys antibodies).
  • Vaccinate dams before birth according to the vet's programme, so colostrum carries antibodies against local disease risks.
  • Agree on volumes, timing and testing (such as colostrum or serum checks) with the herd vet rather than using generic figures.

In poultry, maternal antibodies are transferred through the yolk, so breeder vaccination programmes play the same role.

lessons.title: Housing, nutrition and growth to weaning
lessons.html:
Environment and feeding of young stock

Housing and environment

  • Clean, dry, draught-free bedding; damp bedding drives navel infections and pneumonia.
  • Good ventilation without draughts at animal level – the same principle applies to calf hutches, lambing pens and chick brooders.
  • Supplementary heat for piglets (heated creep areas) and chicks (brooders) according to breed guides, with temperature judged by animal behaviour as well as thermometers.
  • Hygiene between batches: all-in, all-out where possible, cleaning and resting pens.
  • Navel care in calves, lambs and kids as part of a vet-approved protocol.

Nutrition

Young ruminants start as functional monogastrics; milk bypasses the rumen via the oesophageal groove. Rumen development depends on early access to dry feed (starter or creep feed) and clean water, which stimulate microbial fermentation and papillae growth. Practical points:

  • Artificial rearing (dairy calves, orphan lambs): consistent milk or milk replacer concentration, temperature and timing; clean feeding equipment; follow the product label for mixing.
  • Creep feeding of beef calves, lambs and piglets: offers supplementary feed the dam cannot reach, raising weaning weights and easing the weaning transition. Its economics depend on feed price, the value of extra weaning mass and veld condition.
  • Water must be freely available from the first days.

Monitoring growth

Measure birth weight and weigh at fixed intervals or at weaning. Average daily gain and adjusted weaning weights (for example 205-day weights in beef recording) allow comparison against breed and farm targets and support selection decisions. Body condition and growth of young animals reflect both the dam's milk production and the management system.

Weaning

Weaning is a nutritional and social stress. Reduce it by ensuring animals already eat solid feed, weaning at an appropriate age and weight rather than date alone, avoiding other stressors (castration, dehorning, transport, vaccination) at the same time where possible, and providing good-quality feed and shelter afterwards. Fence-line or two-step weaning methods can reduce stress in cattle.

lessons.title: Health, welfare and performance indicators
lessons.html:
Managing health and measuring success

Common juvenile health problems

ProblemMain risk factors
Neonatal diarrhoea (scours)Poor colostrum intake, dirty environment, overcrowding
Navel and joint infectionsDirty birth environment, poor navel care
PneumoniaPoor ventilation, draughts, mixing ages, stress
Hypothermia and starvationCold, wet weather; poor mothering; weak newborns
Coccidiosis and wormsContaminated pens and pastures, high stocking
PredationJackal and caracal in lambing camps; stray dogs

A herd health plan drawn up with the veterinarian should set vaccination, parasite control and treatment protocols. All medicines must be used under veterinary direction or according to the registered label, with withdrawal periods recorded.

Welfare and husbandry procedures

Castration, disbudding or dehorning, tail docking and identification are routine but painful. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 prohibits unnecessary suffering. Best practice is to perform procedures at the youngest appropriate age, by trained staff, with methods and pain control agreed with the vet and in line with industry codes of practice. Predator management in lambing camps (kraaling at night, guard animals, lambing in protected camps) also reduces losses.

Key performance indicators

  • Birth-to-weaning mortality (%) and causes of death.
  • Weaning rate: young weaned per female exposed to breeding.
  • Average weaning weight and average daily gain.
  • Kilograms weaned per breeding female or per hectare.
  • Treatment rate for scours and pneumonia.

Tracking these by season, sire group and management batch reveals where interventions pay. For example, a rise in lamb losses in the first three days points to birth management, mothering and chilling, while losses after a few weeks point to disease or nutrition. Extension officers can use the same indicators to support communal and emerging farmers with practical, low-cost changes such as kraaling, colostrum management and clean pens.

Key points

  • The juvenile phase carries the highest mortality and sets lifetime performance.
  • Early colostrum intake is the most important neonatal intervention because antibody absorption declines quickly after birth.
  • Dry, draught-free, hygienic housing and early access to dry feed and water support health and rumen development.
  • Reduce weaning stress by avoiding other stressors at the same time.
  • Husbandry procedures must be done young, by trained staff, under a vet-approved welfare protocol.
  • Measure mortality, weaning rate and weaning weight to target improvements.

quiz.question: Why must newborn ruminants receive colostrum as early as possible?

options.text: It prevents all diseases for life
The gut's ability to absorb antibodies declines rapidly after birth
Colostrum is needed to start rumen fermentation
Colostrum contains no nutrients after the first day
By leaving it in direct sun
Gently, without overheating, to protect the antibodies

quiz.question: What stimulates rumen development in young ruminants?

options.text: Keeping them off feed until weaning
Early access to dry starter or creep feed and water
Ensuring animals already eat solid feed and avoiding other stressors at the same time
Castrating, vaccinating and transporting on the weaning day
Weaning strictly by calendar date regardless of weight
